chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ahmad ibn Khalid from Abdillah ibn Yahya from Abdillah ibn Muskān from Abū Baṣīr who said:

I said to Abū 'Abdillāh (peace be upon him) regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted and Mighty: 'Zakat is only for the poor and the needy' (1). He said: 'The poor is the one who does not ask people, and the needy is more hard-pressed than him, and the wretched is the most hard-pressed of them. And whatever Allah, Exalted and Mighty, has made obligatory upon you, its public declaration is better than its concealment, and whatever is voluntary, its concealment is better than its public declaration. And if a man were to carry the zakat of his wealth on his shoulder and distribute it publicly, that would be good and beautiful.'

key_terms.الْفَقِيرُ: The poor, defined here as one who does not ask people
key_terms.وَالْبَائِسُ: The wretched, the most hard-pressed of the three categories
key_terms.وَالْمِسْكِينُ: The needy, defined here as more hard-pressed than the poor

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between the poor and the needy in Shia jurisprudence, and how should zakat be distributed?
ai.summary: In this narration from Al-Tusi's *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) provides a nuanced distinction between the poor and the needy, defining the poor as those who do not ask and the needy as those in greater hardship. The hadith establishes a key jurisprudential principle regarding the etiquette of charity: obligatory payments like zakat are superior when declared publicly to encourage others, whereas voluntary charity is better kept secret to preserve humility. This ruling is contextualized within the chapter on the obligation of giving zakat to the Imam, highlighting the public nature of the state's collection and distribution.
